en: The Great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai says that from the passage "The elder saw this great fire" onwards is the second part, the distinct parable (*bipiyi*). This is further divided into four sections:
first, the parable of the elder seeing the fire, which corresponds to the Buddha’s vision of the five turbidities (*pañcakaṣāya*), as expressed in the four lines of verse.

First, the analogy of the original [chariots] serves as the basis; second, the analogy of discarding the small carts for large ones illustrates how Śākyamuni, for the sake of those in the five turbidities, temporarily set aside the Great Vehicle to bestow the Small Vehicle at the beginning of his sitting at the site of enlightenment, with seventeen and a half lines of verse serving as the basis;

third, the analogy of equally bestowing large carts upon all sons illustrates how Śākyamuni reveals the true aspect, saying, "I see my sons who are all equally resolved to seek the Buddha-way," with six lines of verse serving as the basis.
Fourth, the parable of the elder being free from falsehood illustrates the aforementioned statement, "I am the King of all Dharmas," based on two and a half verses.
Regarding the initial sight of the fire, there are four textual passages, though their meaning comprises only three points: first, clarifying the capacity to see;
[second, the act of seeing; third, the result of seeing].
Second, clarifying what was seen;
third, clarifying the fear and terror;
fourth, elaborating upon what was previously seen.
This establishes three points of meaning: "The elder saw" indicates the seer, which is analogous to my own observation with the Buddha-eye;
"a great fire arose from the four sides" indicates that which was seen, which is analogous to the sentient beings of the six realms whom I perceive;
and "he was immediately struck with great alarm and fear" is analogous to the arising of the mind of great compassion for the sake of these sentient beings.
The passage beginning with "And the sons within the burning house" extensively explains the second type of fire perceived therein; it serves to further clarify the meaning of their alarm and fear.

The body, sensations, mind, and phenomena are the four sides of the house; from these four sides arise the four inversions of purity, pleasure, and so forth. The fires of the eight sufferings and all manner of afflictions gather therein; yet, if one knows that the body is impure, suffering, and impermanent, the fire of the afflictions will be extinguished.
There have been three traditional interpretations:
first, that the four great elements constitute the four sides, with the six consciousnesses all relying upon them;
second, that they are the four modes of birth.
Third, regarding the four inversions:
according to the subsequent text, birth, old age, sickness, and death constitute the four extremes.
"Immediately becoming greatly terrified" means that one is startled by the thought of retreating from the Great Goodness (Mahāyāna) and fearful of the prospect of giving rise to grave evils.
"Startled, one immediately faces loving-kindness (*maitrī*), mindful that there is no joy; terrified, one immediately faces compassion (*karuṇā*), grieving that there is suffering.

The phrase "Although I am able to emerge safely from this burning gate" explains the meaning of startlement, terror, loving-kindness, and compassion. Although these are incomplete words, they clarify that the Buddha, by the power of wisdom, is able to seek out the true teachings and perceive the truths they expound. Because he is not endangered by the five turbidities or the eight sufferings, he is called "safe" (*an*). Because he cannot be moved by the violent winds of the four inversions (*viparyāsa*), he is called "secure" (*yin*). Because he is serene and beyond all burdens, he is called "emerged" (*chu*).
Sentient beings are not like this; while they are burned by fire, the Tathāgata’s compassion is instead inflamed by the fire of sorrow, which is why he says "although.
Regarding the passage in the sutra that speaks of "the gates that are burned," I now ask:
"If the teaching constitutes the gate, is this teaching itself being burned?"
"Is it not burned? Jiu replied: "The gate itself is not burned;

Buddhism serves as the gate. It is that which enables the person to pass through who is burned. Because the person being passed through is burned, the gate that enables them to pass is called 'burned. It is like when a person inside a gate dies, the gate is said to have declined, though the gate itself does not actually decline."
He asked again:
"If that is so, then the Teaching must be eternal and not a conditioned phenomenon;
if it is not so, why does it not burn?"
Now, the explanation is as follows:

"It is not so. A gate possesses both the phenomenal (jian) and the empty (kong). Without the phenomenal, there would be nothing to mark the gate; without the empty, there would be no means to penetrate through it. While the phenomenal may be reduced to ashes, the empty cannot be burned."

The teaching consists of the expressive medium (*abhilāpa*) and that which is expressed (*abhidheya*). If there were no expressive discourse, there could be no teaching; if there were nothing to be expressed, how could one attain liberation?
While the expressive discourse may be impermanent, that which is expressed is not impermanent. Because one attains the expressed meaning from beneath the teaching, it is called "attaining peace";
because the expressive medium perishes, it is said that "the gates are burned."
If one does not exit through the gate of that which is burned, by what means can one emerge in safety?
Relying upon the verbal teaching to accord with that which it explicates, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"Because the cause is impermanent, the fruit is permanent. To explain it in this manner is like exiting through the gate of that which is burned as described in the sutra.
If it is the teaching gate of impermanence in the Hīnayāna, one emerges through the gate of that which is burned;

if it is the teaching gate of eternal abiding in the Mahāyāna, where the written word is itself liberation, then this teaching is identical to the principle, and by realizing that there is neither burning nor non-burning, one safely emerges.
If one considers this from the perspective of the Tathāgata’s provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), it is as if emerging through the door of what is being burned;

if one considers it from the perspective of his ultimate wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*), the essence emerges securely from within the burning itself. Therefore, the meaning is that he was first unable to bring them out by means of garments, baskets, or tables, but later brought them out by means of impermanence (*anityatā*).
"Delighting in and clinging to play" (*hikhī*): attachment to views is called "play" (*hikhī*), while attachment to craving is called "sport" (*khī*);
furthermore, being immersed in the four views is called "play," and to squander one's merit and fame is called "sport"—attachment to craving is likewise so.

Being immersed in the five sensory objects (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) is called "play," and to be empty-handed with no gain is called "sport"; to die in vain and repeatedly take birth without weariness or renunciation is like that child’s play.

Regarding "neither perceiving nor knowing": not speaking of the existence of fire at all is called "not perceiving"; not understanding that fire is a phenomenon of heat is called "not knowing. Since one does not know the heat of fire, one does not fear injury to the body—this is called "not being startled. Since one does not worry about the severance of life, one does not feel terror. Sentient beings do not perceive the five aggregates or the eight sufferings at all, nor do they know the four inversions or the three poisons; since they do not recognize these delusions, how could they have any anxiety or concern?

Delusions invade the Dharma-body and wound the life-force of wisdom; thus, one does not awaken to suffering, does not know the origin [of suffering], is not startled by the path, and does not fear the cessation [of suffering]. Because one has not heard the teaching of the Four Noble Truths, one lacks what is called "hearing-wisdom" (śrutamayī-prajñā), which is termed "non-awakening"; one lacks what is called "contemplative wisdom" (cintāmayī-prajñā), which is termed "not knowing.
One lacks what is called "insight through vision," which is termed "non-awakening"; one lacks what is called "insight through contemplation," which is termed "not knowing."
Upon seeing the truths, one is immediately startled into awakening; through reflection, one feels revulsion and fear.

Furthermore, because one does not perceive present suffering nor understand future suffering, the subsequent passage states: "One undergoes manifold sufferings in the present, and later undergoes the sufferings of the hells and so forth"—this is precisely that meaning.
"Afflicted by the body" refers to the five consciousnesses;
"mind" refers to the mental consciousness, which is the sovereign mind (citta-rāja).
It means that while the body is oppressed by the eight kinds of suffering, the mind does not become weary or distressed.

It is also said that they have previously planted the merit of the Mahāyāna; this has the wisdom of the *dharmakāya* as its essence, yet this essence is oppressed by the four inversions (*catur-viparyāsa*), such that it neither knows nor perceives.
"Having no weariness or distress in the mind" means not being weary of the suffering of impermanence and not being distressed by the accumulation of afflictions.
"Having no intention to seek emergence" means not practicing the Path in order to seek cessation.

Now it is said that the burning house is fundamentally a metaphor for the five corruptions (*pañca-kaṣāya*). "Playing" represents the corruption of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*); "sporting" represents the corruption of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*); "not perceiving, not knowing, not being startled, and not fearing" represents the corruption of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*); "the fire coming to press upon the body with piercing pain" represents the corruption of life-span (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*); and "the mind feeling no weariness or distress and lacking the intent to seek escape" represents the corruption of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). These correspond to the five corruptions, and so forth.

From the passage "The elder had this thought" onwards is the second section, the analogy of discarding the small stool to use the carriage. This illustrates the aforementioned case where the great [gift] was intended for the large [recipient] but the small was used instead. The first six lines and a half clarify that the great [gift] could not be obtained;
the subsequent eleven lines clarify that by using the small [gift], it was obtained.
There are three reasons why [the teaching] cannot be given to those of superior capacity:
first, the Great Mind’s contemplation of what is appropriate;
second, the absence of the necessary spiritual capacity (*indriya*).

Third, the cessation of transformation. II. The Section on the Appropriate Application of Exhortation and Admonition.
This consists of three parts each for exhortation and admonition:
first, the appropriate application; [and so forth].
Second, not receiving;
third, relinquishing. The three aspects of the exhortation gate are:
1. From "The elder thought thus: 'My hands and body possess strength'" onwards, this illustrates the aforementioned application of great compassion through contemplation during the twenty-one days;

2. From "He further reflected" onwards, it clarifies that the son did not accept [the gift], which illustrates how sentient beings lacking the capacity have dull faculties and how they might be delivered;

3. From "Or he might fall and be burned by fire" onwards, this represents the relinquishing of skillful guidance, illustrating how, for those lacking the capacity, one ceases the transformative work and thinks, "I would rather not preach the Dharma, but quickly enter nirvana."

The passage beginning with “The elder thought thus” illustrates the aforementioned seven-day period of contemplation. Regarding the phrase “body and hands,” the text cites the subsequent section to harmonize with the analogy, stating:

“By means of the power of spiritual transformations (*ṛddhi*) and the power of wisdom (*prajñā*). This explains the metaphor: the body represents the bearing of the burden through supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), while the hands represent the lifting up through wisdom. Based on the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa*) attained through samādhi, one possesses supernatural powers; based on the virtue of knowledge (*jñāna*) attained through wisdom, one possesses the preaching of the Dharma. The power of this wisdom and cessation can accomplish the *dharmakāya*. Furthermore, this wisdom and cessation enter through two gates: exhortation and admonition. Exhortation corresponds to the *puruṣakāra-siddhānta* (the standpoint for individuals), while admonition corresponds to the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of remedial treatment). These two standpoints serve as the skillful means (*upāya*) for the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the standpoint of ultimate truth).

When the Tathāgata first intended to employ the gate of exhortation to suit sentient beings, seeking to have them practice all that is good so as to achieve the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the knowledge of all modes, sentient beings were unable to bear it.

Next, he intended to employ the gate of admonition to suit them, seeking to have them refrain from all evil and realize Great Nirvāṇa; yet sentient beings were again unable to bear it, as they lacked the capacity and his transformative activity ceased. Thus we know that employing mindfulness according to the Mahāyāna is simply the two *siddhāntas* of exhortation and admonition, which are nothing other than supernatural power, wisdom, and the abandonment of defilements. Therefore, the preceding passage states: "Adorned with the power of concentration and wisdom, one delivers sentient beings by means of these"—this is precisely its meaning.
The previous praise of the elder’s advanced age is a metaphor for wisdom and cessation (*jñāna-prahāṇa*); wisdom and cessation are precisely the strength of his body and hands.
Regarding the "garment-bag and desk," the Tripiṭaka Master says that the *kuci* (garment-bag) is a foreign vessel for holding flowers, used to store offerings presented to persons of high rank.
The old commentary says:

"The lapel of the robe is likened to the cause of the Mahāyāna, and the desk is likened to the fruit of the Mahāyāna; to initially propose the Mahāyāna’s cause and fruit [to such a person] would mean they lack the spiritual capacity."
An earlier source further states:
"This object is a metaphor for the Mahāyāna precepts, concentration, and wisdom; the dharmas obtained through contemplation during the first seven days are like using a cloth bag;
the contemplation of the faculties and conditions of sentient beings during the second seven days is like using a small table."
"Contemplate the kindness of the earth for twenty-one days, as if using a case.
This meaning is said to originate from the *Āgama Sūtras*.

Now, taking the text that provides the analogy: "If I were to praise the Tathāgata’s knowledge, vision, powers, and fearlessness by means of my own supernatural power and the power of wisdom alone, sentient beings would not be able to attain liberation through this."

The power of spiritual transformations (*ṛddhi-bala*) is the body; the power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*) is the hand. As previously stated, knowledge and vision are likened to a garment-bag, fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*) to a small table, and the ten powers (*daśabala*) to a desk. The Tathāgata employs supernatural powers to activate these three dharmas, and through wisdom, he proclaims these three dharmas; when there are no receptive vessels, he ceases his transformative activity.
The distinctions between the brief, the intermediate, and the extensive [explanations] are merely like those between a robe-satchel (*cīvarakaṭhina*), a small table, and a desk.

The brief exposition is called the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision; "knowledge" refers to the *sarvākārajñatā* (all-aspect wisdom), and "vision" refers to the Buddha-eye. Thus, while the names are brief, the meaning is profound, just as a robe-satchel has only one opening yet contains much.

To speak of them in their intermediate form is called the Four Fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*); they correspond to the Four Truths like a small table, being somewhat more extensive regarding the Dharma and somewhat more secure regarding sentient beings.

Alternatively, when explained extensively, they are called the Ten Powers (*daśabala*); they encompass all things both horizontally and vertically, like a desk with many legs that cannot be overturned. Thus, regarding the Dharma they are broad, and regarding sentient beings they are greatly secure. He contemplated for twenty-one days, wishing to present this Dharma of the Buddha in such a manner—both extensive and concise—but as sentient beings could not endure it, he spoke of the "robe-sleeve" and the "table."

"Furthermore, he reflected again," and so forth, constitutes the second section, clarifying that the son did not accept [the teaching], which serves as an analogy for the absence of spiritual capacity (*anabhavyatā*) mentioned above.
"There was but one gate, and it was moreover narrow"—the meaning of the "gate" is as explained previously.
Now, to further clarify the general and the specific:
as for the specific, "one" refers to the single principle, the purity of the one path;
"gate" refers to the correct teaching, which penetrates that which is to be penetrated.
"Small" means that it does not accommodate [views such as] eternalism and nihilism, nor the seven stages of expedient means (*saptaprayoga*).

Since its teachings and principles are vast and extensive, they are not narrow; however, because sentient beings are unable to realize these principles and teachings for themselves, it is said to be "narrow and small" in reference to their lack of capacity.

Regarding "penetration" (tong): because the principle is pure and without admixture, it is called "one" (yi); because this principle can lead one through, it is called a "gate" (men); and because it is subtle and difficult to know, it is called "narrow and small" (xiǎoxiǎo).

As for the teaching: because one seeks throughout the ten directions and finds no other vehicle, but only the Single Buddha Vehicle, it is called "one. Because this teaching can lead one through, it is called a "gate. This teaching is so subtle that ordinary beings do not know its point of exit; this is their ignorance of the provisional. They do not know its point of entry; this is their ignorance of the real.
Those of the Two Vehicles, having heard a little, know the essentials of the exit but never know the entry.

Although Bodhisattvas know the exit for themselves, they likewise do not know the entry. Deprived of the seven expedient means, none of them know either the entry or the exit. As the preceding passage states:
"If I were to praise the Buddha-vehicle, sentient beings would remain submerged in suffering.
Unable to communicate through such teaching, and because they lack the capacity [to understand], he says it is "narrow and small."

The practitioner perfects the cause through their own practice; because they traverse the great, direct path without hindrance, it is called "One. Because they skillfully practice the Bodhisattva path and proceed straight to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), it is called a "gate. Because their wondrous practice involves difficult deeds and skillful means that are beyond the capacity of ordinary faculties, it is merely described as "narrow and small."

The ancient interpretation states that they are called "infants" because their wholesome roots are minor, pertaining only to humans and devas; they are said to be "unaware" because they lack the wholesome roots of the Mahāyāna.

Our current explanation clarifies that although they have been taught the unsurpassed path by twenty thousand Buddhas, their Mahāyāna wholesome roots are so feeble as to be termed "infantile"; furthermore, if upon hearing the Mahāyāna they are able to give rise to slander and revilement, they are termed "unaware."

Regarding the phrase "attached to places of play": the preceding section clarified that goodness is weak, while this section clarifies that evil is strong. This means that at the time of the cause, one is deeply attached to views and craving; at the time of the fruit, one is deeply attached to the primary and secondary realms (the physical body and its environment). In the desire realm, one is attached to the six sense objects; in the form realm, one is attached to the flavor of dhyāna;

and in the formless realm, one is attached to meditative concentration. As the previous text states: "The faculties of sentient beings are dull; blinded by attachment to pleasure and ignorance, they are incapable of hearing the Mahāyāna."
The two phrases, "Or they may fall and be consumed by fire," refer to what is called "abandoning good guidance.
There are two kinds of falling:

first, that of the immature, who fall because they remember their former places of play; second, that of total ignorance, who fall because they grasp at things without firmness—this is analogous to falling into the three miserable realms due to attachment to the five desires.
Second, those who are weak in virtue and lack discernment slander the Mahāyāna and fall into the three miserable realms.
From the passage "preaching for the sake of [instilling] fear" onwards, there are three parts to the second section on the gate of remediation:
first, the remediation through appropriate application.

He warns of fear to urge them toward liberation; the characteristics of this remedy are as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. The four foundations of mindfulness constitute the Mahāyāna because they are ungraspable, and thus differ from the Hīnayāna.
Since they are attached to the locus of play, he speaks of matters of fear so that they may escape being burned by the fires of the five turbidities.

The house of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) should be abandoned; if one dwells attached to it for long, one will surely sever the roots of goodness. Therefore, it is said: "Do not let it be burned and harmed by fire."
From the passage "Although the father feels compassion" onwards, it describes how the son does not accept the admonition.

"Neither startled nor afraid" means that he does not give rise to the hearing and reflection described above; he does not recognize that the eight sufferings and the five turbidities can burn away his roots of goodness, just as one who does not recognize fire;
he does not recognize that the aggregates, elements, and sense bases are the vessels of all suffering, just as one who does not recognize a house.
One does not know the cause for losing the Dharma-body, just as one does not know what has been lost.

From the two phrases, "merely running back and forth in play while looking at his father," these are designated as words of lamentation regarding the abandonment [of the path]. All turning one's back on light and heading toward darkness is like "running back and forth"; the rapid coming and going of birth and death is like "rushing about"; and the arising of views and attachments therein is like "playing. Although one employs great [means] to approximate [the truth], one does not follow the Great Teaching; therefore, it is said, "merely looking at his father."

From the passage, "The elder then thought: 'This house has already been consumed by a great fire,'" onwards constitutes the second parable of the chariot, which illustrates the eleven lines of verse concerning "recalling the power of the skillful means practiced by the Buddhas of the past."
In the preceding passage there were four points, and now the parables are likewise four:

first, the parable of the three carts intended for the purpose, which illustrates the previous statement that "recalling the Buddhas of the past, they also employ the transformation of the three vehicles";

second, the parable of the father knowing the inclinations of his children's hearts, which illustrates the previous statement that "when he thought this, the Buddhas of the ten directions all appeared."

Third, the parable of praising the three vehicles, which illustrates the preceding passage: "Having correctly bestowed the three vehicles and reflected upon this matter, he immediately proceeded to Vārāṇasī.
Fourth, the parable of fulfilling the sons' wishes, which illustrates the preceding passage: "Accepting, practicing, awakening to, and entering [the truth] is called turning the wheel of Dharma."

The transformative merit of the Mahāyāna constitutes the father’s life-force, while the great goodness of sentient beings constitutes the son’s life-force. If great goodness is exhausted, then the son’s life-force is severed; once the son’s life-force is severed, the transformative merit is likewise nullified, and thus the father’s life-force is severed as well.
The preceding statement, "the pain is already acute," implies that one has not yet died; now, saying "one will certainly be burned" carries the meaning of death.
In the previous passage, it was said that one could emerge safely from the burning gate; now it says, "if you do not exit at once, you will certainly be burned. What is the meaning of this?
That which emerged previously was the emergence of the Dharma-body;

what is now said regarding "not emerging at the proper time" refers to the Response-body (nirmāṇakāya) being afflicted by illness. When sentient beings possess goodness, the Response-body emerges at the proper time; when the goodness of sentient beings is severed, the Response-body does not emerge at the proper time. Thus, both cases result in being consumed by fire.
Now, wishing to manifest a responsive body according to what is appropriate, he causes it to appear at this time.
From the passage "I shall now employ skillful means," he intends to establish provisional expedients.
From the passage "Knowing the former mind of his son" onwards is the second section, clarifying that there exists the potential for deliverance.
In the past, some had practiced the Lesser Vehicle; this shows that their prior mental dispositions and inclinations were different, and thus it is known that each has its own preferences.

Furthermore, it is known that some sentient beings had previously practiced the Greater Vehicle, yet because their practice of the Great was not yet deep, they are "weak in the Great. Because they weary of old age, sickness, and death, they are approached with the Lesser Vehicle; this is being "strong in the Lesser," as in the case of Śāriputra, who fell back from six moments of mind. His original practice of the Great is what is meant by "knowing the prior mind," while his intermediate weariness of old age and death is what is meant by "each having its own preferences."

From the passage "and addressed them, saying" onwards, the third section is the parable of the rarity of the three vehicles, which serves as a metaphor for the aforementioned turning of the true wheel of Dharma.
This consists of three parts:
namely, exhortation, revelation, and realization.
The section beginning with "rare and wonderful playthings" constitutes the exhortation to turn [the wheel];
the section beginning with "such various [things]" constitutes the demonstration of turning;
and the section beginning with "You should all quickly come out from this burning house, and I shall give them all to you" constitutes the testimony of turning.

From "At that time, the sons heard what their father said" onwards is the fourth section, the parable of the sons attaining their wishes, which illustrates the aforementioned practice and realization.
While the preceding verse was brief, the present parable is detailed; it extensively clarifies the cultivation of causes leading to the fruit.
The explanation is based on six phrases:
first, "fulfilling one's wishes" refers to the correspondence between the capacity of the recipient and the teaching; this is the wisdom of hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*).

Second, "courageous vigor" refers to the wisdom of reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*); it is the movement of thought and deliberation, which constitutes the skillful means (*upāya*) of the wisdom of reflection.

Regarding "mutually pushing and displacing": one pushes against the four truths to displace and subdue the delusions of view; because right and wrong have not yet been decided, it is called "mutual. This belongs to the stage of applied wisdom (*bhāvanā-prajñā*) and corresponds to the stages of *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*.

"Competing" (jing) means competing to grasp the superior principle; this refers to the stage of the Dharma of Patience (kṣānti-dharma), wherein one competes to grasp the superior principle by first contemplating the thirty-two truths and competing to advance toward the True Path, subsequently contracting the contemplation to advance toward the Dharma-patience regarding suffering (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti).

"Commonality" refers to the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), wherein one contemplates the single Truth equally, without distinction from the four contemplations of the Receptivity to the Dharma of Suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*).

"Rushing forward" refers to entering the fifteen moments of mind within the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*), swiftly perceiving the principle; this is analogous to the aforementioned "immediate sound of Nirvana," signifying that one attains a portion of Nirvana within the Path of Vision.

"Striving for emergence" refers to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); it is the striving to emerge from the triple world to achieve the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣaphala*). Only when the cultivation of thought is exhausted does one finally emerge from the burning house; this corresponds to the aforementioned verse’s mention of "the distinct names of the Arhat, Dharma, and Saṃgha."

Regarding the one who understands through contemplation of the mind: the correct contemplation of the Middle Way directly perceives the true reality (*dharmatā*). When the mind and its phenomena correspond, it is called "fulfilling one's vow.
Because the objective realm is boundless, the contemplation is likewise boundless; this is called "courage."
The mutual investigation of the object and the mind is called "sharpening one another.
The interaction between the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) as they take objects is called "racing together in competition."
To traverse all aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) such that none are not the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is called "leaving the burning house," and so forth.

The passage beginning with "At that time, the elder saw his sons" constitutes the third parable within the distinct similes: the parable of bestowing great chariots equally upon all the sons, which illustrates the aforementioned manifestation of the true reality.
This passage consists of four parts:

First, the parable of the father’s joy upon seeing his sons escape danger. This illustrates the two lines and one phrase of the preceding verse, from "I then had this thought for the reason I appeared in the world" up to "Now I am joyful and fearless.

Second, the parable of the sons seeking vehicles. This illustrates the awakening of the Mahāyāna potential, based on the two lines of the preceding verse: "I see my sons, all of whom are equally resolved to seek the Buddha-way, and they have all come to me with hearts of reverence."

Third, the parable of equally bestowing great chariots upon all the sons illustrates the three preceding lines: "Among all bodhisattvas, he directly abandons expedient means and teaches only the unsurpassed path.
Fourth, the parable of the sons' joy upon receiving the chariots illustrates the preceding verse: "When the bodhisattvas hear this Dharma, the net of their doubts is entirely removed."

In the preceding discourse on the Dharma, it was first explained how the spiritual capacity is awakened, followed by the teaching on the removal of obstacles, the Buddha’s joy, and his fearlessness; now, in this analogy, it is first explained how they escape danger, followed by the seeking of the carriage.
If one were to treat this exhaustively, it should be formulated as four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*):

First, there are cases where hindrances are first removed and subsequently the great capacity (*mahā-indriya*) is awakened; for example, in the Tripitaka, the hindrances of the four great śrāvakas and others were removed, and at the end of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the beginning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, their great capacity was finally awakened.

Second, there are cases where hindrances have not yet been removed but the Mahāyāna capacity is awakened; for example, the various ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* who attained entry into the Buddha’s wisdom. The remaining two propositions are as explained above.

If those of great capacity first activate their spiritual resonance and subsequently have their obstacles removed, it is as described in the "Expedient Means" chapter; if they first have their obstacles removed and subsequently activate their spiritual resonance, it is as described here. These two cases—where the activation of resonance and the removal of obstacles manifest alternately—converge to form a single underlying meaning.

Furthermore, the "Expedient Means" chapter elucidates the Buddha’s joy and fearlessness; here, the sons rejoice, and because the sons rejoice, the father also rejoices. This mutual manifestation serves to demonstrate that they share a single intent.
The state of escaping danger possesses two meanings:
namely, escaping danger and rejoicing.

If the son has not yet escaped danger, the father is filled with anxiety; if he succeeds in leaving the fire, the father’s mind becomes serene. Therefore, escaping danger and rejoicing are treated as a single analogy.
Because the son rejoices, the father also rejoices; this is analogous to the joy of the Buddha.
Regarding the phrase "in the middle of the four-way crossroads," the old explanation states:
the removal of the four turbid obstructions is like a road that reaches in all directions; further, the removal of one additional turbidity is like sitting in the open air.
Now, this is not the case here; the five turbidities (pañca-kaṣāya) directly clarify the nature of defilements and obstacles, without yet discussing the path of cultivation.

Therefore, they should not be compared to a crossroads. A crossroads properly illustrates the Four Noble Truths; the distinct modes of contemplating these truths are called the four directions of the crossroads, while the convergence of the Four Truths at the realization of the truth is like the junction of the roads. Although the delusions of views (dṛṣṭi-kleśa) have been eliminated, the afflictions of cultivation (bhāvanā-kleśa) still remain, and thus it is not called an "open space."

The exhaustion of all volitional thoughts within the three realms is called "the open space"; dwelling in the fruit of realization without further progression is called "sitting"; not being constrained by views or afflictions is called "serene"; and giving rise to the thought of nirvana and a sense of peace and security is called "rejoicing."
"Each addressed their father," and so forth, marks the second section: the parable of requesting the carts.

The text says, "We pray that you grant us three kinds of precious carts. Although the word "request" (索) does not explicitly appear in the text, its meaning is clearly implied by this petitionary phrase. Thus, it is through this request that the act of requesting the carts is made explicit.
Someone said: "The followers of the Two Vehicles seek the vehicle, whereas the Bodhisattvas do not seek it.
He raised ten difficulties to challenge this, the first of which was:
The followers of the Two Vehicles have already exited the triple world and reached the place where the chariots were promised, so they request their respective vehicles;
why then do the Bodhisattvas suddenly request their vehicles before even reaching that promised place?
A second explanation says:
In the Mahāyāna sūtras, there are no bodhisattvas who seek the fruits of the Hīnayāna; thus, we know they do not seek them.
Third, it is said:

from the initial generation of the mind until reaching the stage of the "near-attainment" (upapatti-bhūmi), the bodhisattvas to be transformed are all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who have not yet transcended the triple world (*tridhātuka*); in this sense, they do not seek [the fruits].

The Bodhisattva capable of transformation possesses thirty-three minds; though one observes their inclinations, one’s contemplation is not yet exhaustive. At the thirty-fourth mind, one becomes a Buddha—so from whom would a Buddha seek anything?

Fourth, the fruit of the Two Vehicles lies outside the gate of the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*), while the fruit of Buddhahood lies outside the gate of habitual tendencies and ignorance (*vāsanā-ajñāna*). Because the Two Vehicles have exhausted the active afflictions but do not see the vehicle [of Buddhahood], they seek it;
why then would a Bodhisattva, who has not yet severed habitual tendencies and ignorance, suddenly seek it?

5. To clarify: the two [vehicles] are expedient means and may be called "seeking. As the text says, "This one reality alone is true; the other two are not real. By this inference, there are only two forms of seeking and one form of non-seeking.

Sixth: From the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* onwards until before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, if both the Buddha-cause and the Buddha-fruition were all expedient means (*upāya*), then this bestowing of treasure upon the impoverished son must also be an expedient means. If the bestowing of the wealth were the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*), then since the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and other texts clarify the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*) as already being the reality, why would he suddenly demand more?

7. Regarding the verses in the "Expedient Means" chapter, it describes the past teaching of the Lesser Vehicle as being an expedient means, but it does not describe the Great Vehicle as being an expedient means. One should know that for the sons of the Buddha, the Mahāyāna is not an expedient means; how then could there suddenly be a request for it?
8. As for the three who seek [the vehicle], why is it that they do not understand?
Because there is no understanding, and because there is no such thing as "understanding," we know they do not seek it.

9. Regarding the granting of the vehicle, the text says: "Seeing all sentient beings depart from the suffering of the triple world and attain the bliss of Nirvāṇa, I therefore grant them the Mahāyāna. Since Bodhisattvas do not realize Nirvāṇa, why would they suddenly seek it?

10. Because the sons were sitting at ease, they approached their father and asked for [a gift]; because those of the Two Vehicles have fulfilled the fruit and no longer practice, they can sit at ease and thus may ask.
Since the Bodhisattva’s practice has not ceased, there is no sense of sitting at ease; why then do they suddenly ask?
I refute this by distinguishing between the general and the specific. "Seeking" (*sō*) and "requesting" (*shō*) are synonymous;

when it resides in the mind, it is called seeking; when it resides in the mouth, it is called requesting; and when it resides in the body, it is called begging. It is like a blind person seeking knowledge, a hungry person requesting food, or a lost person asking for directions. For anyone dwelling in a place where they do not understand, how could there be any principle that does not involve seeking?

Because of the request, [the Buddha] granted it; because he granted it, they rejoiced. The current text contains both the request for the teaching and the expression of joy. Among those addressed by the Dharma-teaching, there were twelve hundred people, with Śāriputra at their head, who made three earnest requests.

Among the assembly of Bodhisattvas, Maitreya was at their head—those born from the Buddha’s own mouth, numbering approximately eighty thousand—who joined their palms with reverent hearts, desiring to hear the complete path. At the beginning of the parables, Śāriputra requested on behalf of those of middling faculties; furthermore, he requested on behalf of the fourfold assembly in general, and incidentally for those of inferior faculties.
The text says: "Excellent, World-Honored One! We pray that you will explain the causes and conditions for the sake of the fourfold assembly."
Regarding the permission granted through the discourse on the Dharma, it says:
"Since you have earnestly requested three times, how could I not speak?
Regarding the permission granted through the parable, it says:
"This meaning should be further clarified through a parable.
The Karmapratyaya-ānujñāta said:
"I shall now speak of the karmic conditions from past lives between myself and you all."
When the discourse on the Dharma was concluded, Śāriputra rejoiced;
when the discourse by way of parables was concluded, Kāśyapa and the others rejoiced;
when the discourse on past lives was concluded, Rāhula rejoiced.
Furthermore, the corresponding passage in the parable states:

"I shall cause my sons to constantly engage in play day and night throughout kalpas, and together with the bodhisattvas, they shall mount this precious vehicle and proceed directly to the site of enlightenment."

Because of joy, one knows there is giving; because of giving, one knows there is an invitation. Since these three cycles and three meanings are clearly and brilliantly manifest, for what reason do you speak only of two instances of seeking and one instance of not seeking?

A separate refutation: first, the Tripiṭaka Master of Qi clarifies that Bodhisattvas do not sever afflictions. Based on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there are four propositions: namely, the movement of the great capacity when obstacles have been removed; the movement of the great capacity when obstacles have not yet been removed; and the knowledge of seeking [the truth] once the capacity has moved.
The second point states:
In Mahāyāna sūtras, there are no bodhisattvas who seek the fruits of the Hīnayāna. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:

"Those of the three vehicles all, by means of the path of ineffable speech, sever afflictions and enter nirvāṇa. Since they are identical in severing afflictions and entering nirvāṇa, why would they not seek [the Mahāyāna]?

The third point states: "Thirty-three minds are called those of a Bodhisattva; at the thirty-fourth, when the afflictions of thought are exhausted, one immediately attains Buddhahood. From whom would a Buddha seek [anything]? This still follows the meaning of the Tripiṭaka:

as long as the obstacles of views have not been eliminated, the great capacity [of the practitioner] still moves. How much more so for the thirty-three minds—how could they be unmoving? If there is movement, one knows that there is seeking.

Fourth, since Bodhisattvas have not yet severed their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and ignorance (*ajñāna*), they should not seek [the fruit]; only when these are completely severed does one become a Buddha. If even a Buddha has no one from whom to seek it, how much less so for those with residual habits and ignorance?

This is the meaning of the Shared Teaching (*sāmānyayāna*) of the Three Vehicles: if even those still bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*) possess such great spiritual capacity (*mahā-indriya*) as to be moved, how much more so those with only residual habits and ignorance?
The fifth point: "This alone is the one reality. Reality is precisely the True; why then do you suddenly seek it elsewhere?

This "one" that is absolute and beyond all dependence has no phenomenon outside of itself. The "one" of the past, which was dependent upon a duality, had phenomena existing outside of itself; though the name is the same, the essence is different. To blindly cling to shards and pebbles, or to fish-eyes, mistaking them for moonstones or the shape of the moon—how can the ignorant be anything but objects of pity for the wise? And so forth.

Regarding the sixth point: from the *Prajñāpāramitā* up to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it is identical to the "entrusting of the Dharma-treasure" (付財法), and thus there should be no seeking [of further teachings].
Have you not heard that regarding common (*sādhāraṇa*) and uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) *prajñā*, one need not seek the uncommon, while for the common, one should not fail to seek it? And so forth.

Regarding the seventh point: at the beginning of the "Expedient Means" chapter, it was previously stated that the Small [Vehicle] is an expedient means; however, it was not mentioned that the previous teaching of the Great [Vehicle] is an expedient means, nor that the Great [Vehicle] is not an expedient means. For this reason, those who do not seek [the Great Vehicle].

Have you not heard in the "Chapter on the Lifespan" that I attained supreme enlightenment after leaving home at a young age? Furthermore, everything that occurred in the interim—whether small or great, whether concerning myself or others—was all my skillful means; the same is true for all Buddhas. How could one not seek this?
The eighth point: If a bodhisattva seeks [understanding], the bodhisattva should comprehend it; since there is no such comprehension, one knows that they do not seek it.

Have you not heard how, when the Dharma teaching was concluded, the assembly of devas, nāgas, and the fourfold assembly all comprehended it? As for those who are not bodhisattvas, what do you think they are?

Furthermore, in the "Dharma Master" chapter, all three vehicles are granted predictions. If they did not understand and accept [the teaching], why would they suddenly be granted predictions? As for the ninth point:

having emerged from the suffering of the triple world and attained the bliss of peace and security, one is then either bestowed with or seeks [the fruit]. Since Bodhisattvas have not yet emerged or realized this, they do not seek it; thus, this remains merely the meaning of the Tripitaka.

As for that tenth point: it is only when the sons are seated at ease that the chariots are bestowed. "Seated at ease" refers to the cessation of movement in the two vehicles; the Bodhisattva's practice is one of non-cessation and is not "seated at ease. Why, then, do you suddenly demand the chariots?
This is merely the same principle as before.

There are those who seek through practice and those who do not seek through practice; furthermore, the practice of a bodhisattva is itself the vehicle, for the vehicle is obtained by means of seeking. How can it be said that one does not seek?

Observing that you have distorted the Three Piṭakas, I have set forth these ten difficulties; yet your narrow perspective sees but a single fragment and fails to grasp the grand scheme. I shall now explain them to you in detail.
There are those who have not severed delusions and do not seek the vehicle—these are the *piṭaka-traya* (Tripiṭaka) bodhisattvas;
there are those who have severed delusions and seek the vehicle—these are the bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*);
and there are those who both sever and do not sever delusions, and both seek and do not seek the vehicle—these are the bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*).
There is that which is neither the severing of delusions nor the non-severing of delusions, neither seeking nor non-seeking; this refers to the Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
Furthermore, there are the five flavors (*wumi*);
within the flavor of milk (*rushi*), there are two meanings:
First, both cutting off and not cutting off, both seeking and not seeking; second, neither cutting off nor not cutting off, neither seeking nor not seeking;
the flavor of curd corresponds to the single intention of neither cutting off nor seeking;
fresh butter encompasses all four intentions.
The refined butter (*ghṛta*) consists of three meanings;
the clarified butter (*sarpis*) consists of one meaning.
Such is the significance of these grand principles and great outlines.
Regarding each and every phrase and each and every meaning, there are further four phrases each:

namely, the movement of the faculty when obstacles have been removed; the movement of the faculty when obstacles have not yet been removed; the movement of the faculty when obstacles have both been removed and not yet removed; and the movement of the faculty when obstacles have neither been removed nor not removed.
This school does not perceive that they cling to "one" while rejecting "three," which is truly to be lamented.

Worldly people, clinging to different enumerations of the chariot and asserting different natures for the chariot, some say that the three chariots were first taught and later the two were merged into one;
others say that there were originally three and later the three were merged into one.
Some say that initially there were four [teachings], but later they were unified into three.

Therefore, when sutras are produced, one should not rely on human words. This text cites how in the past the Buddha taught the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for the śrāvakas, the Dharma of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination for the pratyekabuddhas, and the Dharma of the Six Pāramitās for the bodhisattvas; the number of teachings the present Buddha now speaks of as "three" follows this same principle.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, fascicle eight, states:
"For those who are inferior and weary of the world, he reveals the path of the śrāvaka;
for those with dull faculties who delight in causes and conditions, he explains the path of the pratyekabuddha."
"To those with sharp faculties and compassion, he speaks of the Bodhisattva path;
for the great matter of supreme bliss, he speaks of the immeasurable Buddha-dharma.
(36) Furthermore, it says:

“The three gates of liberation give rise to the Śrāvaka vehicle; the dharma of non-contention gives rise to the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; the six perfections and the four means of integration give rise to the Mahāyāna; and the knowledge of all dharmas gives rise to the Buddha vehicle.”
Furthermore, the ninth stage explains the characteristics of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, the Bodhisattva vehicle, and the Tathāgata vehicle.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*’s commentary on the second stage observes that the accumulation of the ten unwholesome actions leads to falling into the three miserable realms, while the accumulation of the ten wholesome actions results in rebirth in the heavens.

When the aforementioned ten wholesome paths of action are combined with the wisdom of contemplating the Four Noble Truths, one becomes a Śrāvaka; furthermore, when the aforementioned ten wholesome paths of action are combined with the wisdom of contemplation that does not rely on hearing from others, one becomes a Pratyekabuddha; furthermore, when the aforementioned ten wholesome paths of action are combined with the wisdom of fully perfected purity, one attains the stage of a Bodhisattva; and furthermore, when the supreme ten wholesome paths of action are combined with all aspects of all Buddha-dharmas, one becomes a Buddha.
The *Ākāśagarbha-vaipulya-sūtra* (Yíngluò jīng), fascicle 13, states:

"The Buddhas of the ten directions teach the three vehicles; within the One Vehicle, they further open up three, making nine vehicles in total, all of which ultimately converge into the Great Wisdom of Equality."

The Sage spoke thus, yet [his followers] are unable to harmonize these teachings; they engage in mutual contention over right and wrong, disparaging the Dharma and slandering others—there can be no greater fault than this.
Now, I shall differentiate them according to their respective teachings.
If it is taught that while the dharma-gates of the Three Vehicles differ, their ultimate truth is the same, this is the Tripitaka Teaching;
if it is taught that the dharma-gates of the Three Vehicles are the same and their ultimate truths are all the same, this is the Shared Teaching;

if it is taught that there are three times three or nine vehicles, or that the four vehicles have distinct shallow and deep stages each different from the others, yet all enter equally into the Great Wisdom of Equality, this is the Distinct Teaching.

If it is taught that each of the three vehicles, nine vehicles, and four vehicles is individually endowed with the great wisdom of equality, being non-dual and without distinction, this is the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
Furthermore, when analyzed according to the sequence of the five flavors:
in the flavor of milk, only the Bodhisattva Vehicle and the Buddha Vehicle are clarified.
The flavor of curd (*dadhi*) clarifies only the distinctions between the three vehicles;
the flavor of fresh butter (*navanīta*) fully elucidates the respective boundaries of the three, four, and nine vehicles, ensuring they do not overlap;
the flavor of processed butter (*ghṛta*) excludes only what differs from the three vehicles, while the rest is as in the case of fresh butter.
Within the *paramārtha-ghṛta* (the supreme cream), the Buddha-vehicle alone is taught, with no other vehicles remaining.
If one understands this intent, there is no hindrance to differing explanations; if one does not, it merely increases contention and debate.

The people of the world understand that the vehicles of the Buddha-dharma differ in their essential natures. Guangzhai takes the ultimate attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood—the two types of wisdom of non-arising and exhaustion—as the body of the vehicle; compared to the former [teachings], this extends five hundred *yojanas* further, and thus is "high"; it fully contains ten thousand virtues, and thus, compared to the former, is "vast."
The cause for this adornment takes the ten thousand practices as its essence; seeking the supreme above constitutes its height, while transforming those below constitutes its breadth.
The older tradition did not take merit as its essence, because merit is shared with ordinary beings; it took only wisdom as its essence.
Furthermore, the ancient masters held that merit and wisdom together constitute the essence [of the vehicle].

The text states: "They mounted these three chariots," and that they "delighted themselves with the untainted faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, path, meditative concentrations, liberations, and samādhis. How could this refer to wisdom alone?

Furthermore, another master takes only "understanding that exists" (*sajñā*) as the essence [of the vehicle], not taking "understanding of emptiness" (*śūnyatājñāna*) because it is immovable; thus, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) constitute this "understanding that exists.

Moreover, a certain follower of the Hīnayāna takes the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatāprajñā*) as the essence of the vehicle, for the text says: "We have practiced the dharma of emptiness throughout the long night," and so forth.
The Mahāyāna likewise takes true wisdom and skillful means as the body of the vehicle; the body of the vehicle is likened to "existence" (bhava), because existence possesses motion.

I privately remark that when various masters explain the essence of the Buddha-vehicle, they compete to point to the possession of the perfections (pāramitās); how is this different from a group of blind men touching an elephant and disputing over its tail or tusks?

According to the Tiantai master Zhizhe, the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is precisely the body of the chariot, while all the various jewels and ornaments are merely its adornments; this point shall be clarified within the section on the bestowal of the chariot.
The ancient commentary states:

"The small chariot" refers to the small fruit (*phala*). Since this fruit possesses both conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) merits, it specifically takes the conditioned to serve as a metaphor for the movement of the chariot, which carries one into the state of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

Within the conditioned fruit (*saṃskṛta-phala*), both merit (*puṇya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are present; wisdom serves as the primary factor, while merit belongs to the auxiliary perfections (*pāramitā*). This wisdom consists of ten types: eight knowledges (*jñāna*) pertain to both cause and fruit, whereas the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) belong exclusively to the stage of the fruit. Thus, taking these two knowledges as a metaphor for the "fruit of the chariot," for this reason the chariot is situated outside the gate.
If one relies on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, it says:
"This vehicle departs from the triple world and dwells within *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge).

If [the children] have already boarded this vehicle while not yet having departed [from the house], and were vying to leave the burning house, for what reason does it further state that the vehicles are outside the gate?
If it were already outside beforehand, by what means would it have emerged? Rather, it simply refers to the vehicle of the cause and effect:

the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment that sever the delusions of views and thought are all the vehicle of the cause; the knowledge of the exhaustion of non-arising is all called the vehicle of the fruit. One must first rely on the vehicle of the cause to sever and exhaust all delusions before one can attain the vehicle of the fruit—the knowledge of the exhaustion of non-arising; therefore, it is said that "the carriage is outside the gate."
However, while the cause is primary and the fruit secondary, we speak in terms of the fruit when saying "the carriage is outside the gate.
If the internal cause is that which severs the fetters and has the sense of "transporting," then how can the external fruit, which does not transport, be called a "vehicle"?

However, if there were no activity of severing delusions within the fruit, one would have to wait until the attainment of the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising to enter the nirvana without remainder before it could be considered a true attainment;
if one had already reached the fruit by means of the causes, for what reason would one then seek a vehicle?
The ancients said:
"The cord of the mechanism and the cord of sentiment.
The cord of the mechanism can be untied;

Regarding those who seek through emotion: the Buddha taught the doctrine of the extinction of outflows and non-arising. Arhats who have realized this fruit used their supernormal powers and the divine eye to examine the future, yet they still saw the vast expanse of the death and rebirth of transformation. They then doubted the realization of extinction and non-arising they had attained, wondering: "If it were truly non-arising, why do I see existence?"

As it was vast and grand, what was previously not ultimate was sought from the Buddha within the realm of emotional attachment; this is "seeking through emotion. If one searches the scriptural text, these words are not there; if one investigates the meaning, the meaning should not be so; as the text contains nothing that can be interpreted [in that way], it is untenable.
Regarding the term "inference" (or "deduction"), the subsequent text states:

"One gives rise to the notion of nirvana regarding what has been attained. Since one perceives the existence of birth and death with the divine eye, for what reason does one further give rise to the notion of nirvana?
This is self-contradictory.

Furthermore, regarding the Arhats after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if they were unable to reach a definitive understanding because they did not encounter another Buddha, why would it be necessary for them to see a Buddha to reach such understanding when they themselves already perceive birth and death with their divine eye?
Furthermore, the divine eye of the first dhyāna cannot even see the second dhyāna, much less perceive the transformation-death (pariṇāma-cyuti).
This also contradicts the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.

Moreover, if an Arhat who has attained untainted karma were to use the divine eye to see the future birth-and-death retribution of transformation-death, then a person practicing the five precepts and ten wholesome paths should likewise be able to see their own future retribution.
One should know that the retribution outside the realms—how could it possibly be seen by the divine eye?
One must not use this to judge the "emotional rope" (the attachment to one's own realization).

Now, regarding this "emotional rope": in the past, relying on the teachings, one claimed that through the exhaustion of birth and non-arising, one could enter the remainderless nirvana. Yet, within the Vaipulya sutras, one beholds the inconceivable power of the Bodhisattvas and hears the censure of Vimalakīrti; [one reflects: "If what I have attained were truly real, the Great Being should not have humiliated me."
If "I" were not real, the Buddha would not have spoken of the Truth;
therefore, it is said that one is bewildered and does not know what is being said.

Upon reaching the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (the *Dapin*), one comprehends the Great Dharma; hearing this, joy in the Great arises and one intends to advance in the cultivation of the Mahāyāna, yet one cannot yet discern whether one has attained it or not—all such states are already seeking the meaning of the Mahāyāna within the realm of emotional consciousness.
Therefore, Śāriputra, having attained understanding, brought forth his former doubts:

"Seeing all the bodhisattvas receive predictions of their future buddhahood, yet not being included in this matter, I reproach myself with 'Alas! and wish to ask the World-Honored One: have I failed, or have I not?"
This refers to the fact that in the past, during the Vaipulya period, there was already the "seeking by mind.

Now, the addition of "seeking by speech" means that upon hearing the first verse of the "Expedient Means" chapter, they briefly heard the Buddha state that all [teachings] were expedient means; they immediately became attached to these current expedients and doubted whether the past teachings had reached the ultimate.

Thus they said, "I do not now know where this meaning leads," and moved by their long-standing doubts, they spoke three requests to seek the reality of what was taught in the past. Their capacity lay in the Mahāyāna, and their heart sought the truth of the past.
Furthermore, while their hearts seek the Mahāyāna, their mouths inquire about past realities; this is the general principle for the six perfections and the shared teachings.

From the passage "At that time, Śāriputra... onwards, there are three sections concerning the equal bestowal of the great chariots, which consist of two chapters, two expansions, and two explanations:
first, the equality of the sons; second, the equality of the chariots.

Because [all] sons are equal, their minds are equal; this is like all sentient beings equally possessing Buddha-nature: because Buddha-nature is the same, they are all equally sons. Regarding the equality of the second chariot:
because the Dharma is equal, there is nothing that is not the Buddha-Dharma; this is like all dharmas being the Mahāyāna: because the Mahāyāna is the same, they are all equally great chariots.

As for the phrase "each was given," it means that according to their respective original practices of the Four Truths, the Six Perfections, and the immeasurable dharmas, each was shown the reality within their own former training; because these former practices were different, it says "each," and because they are all Mahāyāna, it says "great chariots."

Regarding the passage "Its carriage was high" and below: the broad discussion of the carriage is divided into two parts. First, there is a general description of the carriage's body; second, an explanation of the reasons for possessing such a carriage.
Within the description of the carriage's body, the height and breadth are described first, followed by the explanation of the white oxen, and finally the explanation of the attendants.

The provisional designation of a "chariot" possesses the characteristics of height and breadth; likewise, the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are profound and far-reaching, extending horizontally to the very limits of the Dharma-realm and penetrating vertically to the source and bottom of the Three Truths; therefore, it is said to be "high and broad."
"Adorned with various jewels" is a metaphor for the cultivation and refinement of the myriad practices (*sāhasra-caryā*).
"Surrounded by railings" is a metaphor for *dhāraṇī*, which upholds all that is wholesome and wards off all that is evil.
"The bells suspended on all four sides" is a metaphor for the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) used to transform those below.

"Spreading out the canopy and awning" is a metaphor for the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*); among all virtues, compassion (*karuṇā*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*) are supreme, universally covering all beings.
Regarding the phrase "adorned with rare and miscellaneous jewels," it means that the myriad genuine virtues adorn this compassion. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"If compassion is fully endowed with the ten powers and the fearlessnesses, it is called the Tathāgata’s compassion; within this compassion, one practices giving and so forth," and so on.
"Interlaced with jeweled cords" is a metaphor for the firm great compassionate mind of the Four Great Vows.

"Hanging with various flower tassels" is a metaphor for gladdening and moving sentient beings through the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and it is also a metaphor for the exquisite garland of the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).
"Layering the fine cushions" is a metaphor for the practice of contemplating, refining, and cultivating all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), which are successively stacked and supple.
"Placing the vermilion pillow" means that when a carriage is driven, this support must be raised wherever it goes; this is a metaphor for being still while moving, and moving while still.
If there is a pillow within the carriage, it serves to rest the body and head; this is analogous to how the *ekavyūha-samādhi* (one-practice samādhi) brings rest to all-knowledge and all practices.
"Crimson" (*dan*) refers to red light, which is analogous to the dharma of non-discrimination.
"Riding in a vehicle drawn by white oxen" is a metaphor for how untainted *prajñā* (wisdom) can lead one across the truths and conditions to all practices, reaching *sarvajñā* (omniscience).

White is the fundamental color; thus, it corresponds to original purity and the absence of outflows (*anāsrava*). Its essence possesses myriad virtues, like "plump skin," and it is unstained by afflictions (*kleśa*), like "pure color."

Furthermore, the four foundations of mindfulness are like white oxen; within the four right efforts, the fulfillment of the two types of worldly goodness is like the fullness of the hide, and the exhaustion of the two types of worldly evil is like the purity of its color.
The four bases of psychic power accord with the practitioner’s mind, like "the beauty of one's physical form."
“Sinews” (ṛju) are a metaphor for the five faculties (pañcendriya), in the sense of being firmly established and capable of generating [spiritual power].
“Strength” (bala) is a metaphor for the five powers (pañcabala), in the sense of their function as a trunk that subdues and overcomes.

“Walking with even steps” is used as a metaphor for the equilibrium of meditative concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (prajñā), and also as a metaphor for the balanced harmony of the seven factors of enlightenment (saptabodhyaṅga).
"Swift as the wind" means that by practicing within the Eightfold Noble Path, one swiftly reaches *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).

"Servants and attendants" is a metaphor for the *upāya-pāramitā* (perfection of skillful means), which is able to adapt and follow others in service and obedience; all the various māras, non-Buddhists, and the limited practices of the two vehicles follow the functional application of the wisdom of skillful means.
Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "All are my attendants."
Furthermore, the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) at the stage of fruition that operate according to one’s will are like servants.

Next, from the phrase "Why is this so? onwards, the reason for possessing the chariot is explained: it is because his wealth and treasuries overflow, which is a metaphor for the perfection of merit and wisdom at the stage of fruition; thus, his wealth is said to be immeasurable.
The treasuries are overflowing—the treasury of practice and the treasury of principle—and all dharmas tend toward giving, morality, patience, and so forth.
That which does not transcend this tendency refers to the Tathāgatagarbha in terms of practice; all dharmas tend toward the aggregates, sense bases, elements, faculties, objects, and so forth.
This "not exceeding" refers to elucidating the *tathāgatagarbha* by way of principle.

Practicing this path for oneself is called "filling"; transforming others is called "overflowing. The fulfillment of ultimate wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) is called "filling," while the function of provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) is called "overflowing. Entering the Middle Way is called "filling," and illuminating both simultaneously is called "overflowing."
Not only are the treasuries numerous, but they are all overflowing; what dharma, then, is not the Mahāyāna?
Therefore, the Great Vehicle is immeasurable.
The section beginning with "and he forms this thought" extensively elucidates the mind and so forth; the text is divided into two parts:
First, the equality of the broad mind and so forth; second, the explanation.
Regarding "the equality of the broad mind and so forth": because his wealth is immeasurable and his sons are without partiality, his mind is equal;
if one were wealthy but not a son, or if one were a son but poor, then equality would not be attained.
Now, regarding the statement that "the number of great seven-jeweled carriages is immeasurable," both their teaching and practice constitute the Mahāyāna; this is what is meant by "abundant wealth.

As for the phrase "each is given one, without distinction," it means that without displacing their original training, they are shown the reality: for instance, Śāriputra opened the Buddha’s knowledge and vision through wisdom and became endowed with all Buddha-dharmas;
Maudgalyāyana opened the Buddha’s knowledge and vision through meditative concentration and became endowed with all Buddha-dharmas; others are to be understood in the same way.

Furthermore, in the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā sūtras, various different names—such as the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path—all reveal the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa). This is likewise the case throughout all dharmas; therefore, they are said to be "immeasurable."
"Why is this so? Because I... and below is the explanation of the two kinds of equality.
First, the explanation of the abundance of wealth.

"Even a single country is already vast, how much more so the various sons? This is an analogy for how the great causal principle universally encompasses both good and evil; how much more so the Buddha’s knowledge and vision?
Next, regarding the explanation of "sons" and so forth: if even those who are not sons are already sufficient, how much more so those who are actual sons?
If even those without a karmic connection are saved by the Buddha, how much more so his own children who possess such a connection?

This can be understood by examining the text. From the passage, "At that time, each of the sons mounted a great carriage," onwards is the fourth section: the fulfillment of their wishes and their joy. This is analogous to the aforementioned stages of receiving, practicing, awakening, and entering. Originally they sought rams, deer, and water buffaloes, hoping merely to escape the realm of segmented birth (*bhavāgra*); now they have obtained white oxen that exhaust the realm of changeable birth (*pariṇāmika-nirvāṇa*). Since this exceeds what they originally hoped for, how could they not be joyful?
From "What do you think? onwards is the fourth section, the analogy of non-falsity, illustrating that the Dharma King does not speak falsely;
it consists of three parts: first, the question; second, the answer; and third, the praise.
The question follows the text.
From the words "Śāriputra said" onwards is the second part, the answer, which is divided into two sections:
first, the non-falsity of avoiding the difficulty; this is also called the non-falsity of "substituting the heavy for the light."
Second, "not being at variance with one's original intention" means not being false; it is also called "not being false in exceeding one's original expectations.
Each of these consists of three parts: the heading, the explanation, and the concluding corroboration.
The heading on "avoiding calamity" is as stated in the text.

Regarding the second section, the explanation beginning with "For what reason," [it means that] since life is weighty while the body is light, by preserving the whole body one avoids the fire; having already obtained great treasures to save this precious life, how could there be anything false?

To have escaped the fires of the eight sufferings and preserved the body of the five aggregates is already a great treasure; how much more so this perfect cause for the life-force of Mahayana wisdom from twenty thousand Buddhas, which brings to fulfillment the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—how could this possibly be false?

Next, from "World-Honored One, if it were thus" onwards is the second section, "Not Contradicting One's Original Mind. First is the heading for the chapter on not contradicting one's original mind. Since one originally knows that there are no three [vehicles], the intention is to prevent slander; by not slandering, one has already not contradicted one's original mind.

The commentary states: "Fundamentally, there is no 'small' [vehicle] to be known; the intention is to prevent one from being ruined and falling into evil. Since the cause of ruin does not exist, one does not fall into the fruit of evil. Thus, not providing a small vehicle does not contradict the original intent."

The conclusion states: Knowing for himself that his wealth was immeasurable, and wishing to benefit his sons, he gave them a great carriage exceeding their original expectations; therefore, it was not in vain.

The conclusion of the preceding chapter states, "delivering through skillful means," which seems to illustrate the power of the *prahāṇa-guṇa* (the virtue of abandonment) and supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*).
The conclusion of the subsequent chapter states, "immeasurable wealth," which seems to illustrate the power of the *jñāna-guṇa* (the virtue of wisdom) and eloquent exposition (*pratibhāna*).
The former [part] concerns the children and thus is not in vain; the latter concerns wealth and thus is not in vain.
From "The Buddha told Śāriputra" onwards is the third section, the eulogy, which contains two instances of "Excellent," praising those two aspects of being not in vain.
Question:
Why does the Buddha not himself state that [his words] are not false? Answer:
The Buddha permitted three [people] and one; he himself declared this to be difficult.
Śāriputra’s statement that it is not false makes it easy to gain faith.
From the passage "Śāriputra, the Tathāgata likewise... onwards is the second section: the synthesis of the parable.

Guangzhai set forth ten analogies, yet he harmonized only seven and not three; within those seven, he correctly harmonized five—namely, the fifth and the eighth—but failed to harmonize the seventh and the ninth. Thus, we know that the ten analogies were prolix and lacked coherence.
Now, combining the two analogies—the general and the specific—there are six points within the general analogy, all of which are now integrated in this text, though not in their original order.

First, the first point corresponds to the first [of the specific] above. In the preceding text, the elder’s name, rank, title, and virtuous deeds were mentioned; here, it says, "The Tathāgata is also like this. First, the rank and title are combined: the Tathāgata’s immeasurable virtuous titles briefly cite ten meanings as explained above.

Regarding "all worlds" (*sarvaloka*): taking the location as the definitive name for the practice, whereas above it was stated "countries, cities, and villages," here it is directly termed "all worlds. This collectively refers to the *sahā-lokadhātu* (the realm of endurance), the *abhirati-lokadhātu* (the realm of ultimate bliss), and the *svabhāva-lokadhātu* (the realm of self-nature). All of these are places that are the retribution of wondrous form and wondrous mind; the Tathāgata universally responds in these three places, which constitutes "all worlds" in conjunction with the aforementioned "countries, cities, and villages."

The passage beginning with "Regarding all fears" below combines the preceding praise of both internal and external virtues. Internally, this refers to being advanced in years and in decline; yet in terms of discernment, one possesses great proficiency—just like the Tathāgata’s wisdom and abandonment, wherein ignorance regarding all fears is eternally exhausted. This combines the aforementioned "decline" to manifest the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa*).
"Attaining immeasurable knowledge and vision" combines with his advanced age to manifest his eminent wisdom and virtue;
"the powers," "the fearlessnesses," and so forth, combine with the aforementioned external virtues to signify his immeasurable wealth.

"Power of supernormal faculties" (*ṛddhibala*) refers to being able to attain the superknowledges through the profound cultivation of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); this corresponds to the superior field.
"Power of wisdom" (*prajñābala*) means that wisdom necessarily illumines its objects, just as a body requires a dwelling place; this corresponds to the superior house.
“Endowed with the perfection of skillful means” combines with the aforementioned attendants.

From “great kindness and great compassion” downward, the second section combines with the fourth; for kindness and compassion are the foundation of transformation through giving. “All” refers to the five paths of existence, which are constantly enveloped by kindness and compassion; this combines with the aforementioned five hundred people.
